To manage medications that prolong QT interval, a systematic stepwise approach is required, particularly for high-risk patients.

## Initial Assessment and Risk Stratification

Review concomitant medications for other QT-prolonging agents and any factors affecting drug metabolism, such as renal or liver failure [doc1].

## Dosing and Baseline ECG Monitoring

If a high-risk patient requires QT-prolonging medication after careful assessment, start with the lowest effective dose and adjust according to clinical need [doc1]. Some authorities recommend obtaining a baseline ECG; if baseline QT is prolonged, repeat ECG monitoring after 5 half-lives of the prescribed drug or after any dosage adjustment [doc1]. There are no data supporting routine surveillance ECGs if baseline QTc is normal [doc1].

## Ongoing Monitoring and Patient Education

A QTc interval >500 milliseconds or QTc prolongation >60 milliseconds from baseline warrants careful reassessment [doc1]. Monitor serum potassium and magnesium in patients on multiple QT-prolonging therapies [doc1]. Instruct patients to report new symptoms (palpitations, dyspnea, dizziness) and conditions that could cause hypokalemia, such as gastroenteritis or diuretic use [doc1].

Using two or more QT-prolonging medications does not necessarily cause additional QT prolongation or arrhythmias [doc1]. In a large study of 3,442 patients on QT-prolonging antibiotics, 38.7% were also taking other TdP-inducing drugs, 14% used more than three QT-prolonging medications, and despite 15.9% having hypokalemia, no cases of TdP occurred [doc1].
